description_full: Sprott Inc. is a publicly owned asset management holding company. Through its subsidiaries, the firm provides asset management, portfolio management, wealth management, fund management, and administrative and consulting services to its clients. It offers mutual funds, hedge funds, and offshore funds, along with managed accounts. Further, the firm also provides broker-dealer activities. Sprott Inc. was formed on February 13, 2008, and is based in Toronto, Canada.
ceo_bio: Mr. William Whitney George | CEO & Director | Age 67 | Compensation: $2.6M (FY2025)
culture_narrative: Employs approximately 131 people. Revenue per employee of $2.2M ranks in the top quartile among Financial Services peers, improving at 19%/yr — growing workforce leverage. Each employee generates $732K of free cash flow annually. CEO compensation is 1× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags elevated compensation governance risk (7/10).
financial_summary: Sprott Inc. is a mid-cap financial services business with a $2.9B market cap on $285M of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +25% over the past three years, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder.
Returns on capital run at 15% against a 9% cost of capital, a 6-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it.

The business throws off $96M in free cash flow — roughly 34 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.45× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage of 75× is fortress-like.
Shareholder yield is only 1.2%, a thin return of capital, and insiders hold 6.0% of the shares.

sector_headwinds.text: Price sits 57% above estimated fair value — no margin of safety left, and the cushion against estimate error has been bid away (confirmed by 2 other valuation measures)

Credit cycles and regulatory capital — losses accumulate invisibly in good years and appear all at once, and the time to worry is when underwriting standards are loosest.
Fintech disintermediation — neobanks, embedded finance, and blockchain rails are unbundling the fee streams that traditional banks took for granted.
Interest rate regime shifts — a rapid move in rates can invert the yield curve, crush bond portfolios, and trigger deposit flight simultaneously.

12 consecutive years of dividend payments — an operating record that makes the dividend claim credible
Healthy payout ratio leaves room for both dividend growth and reinvestment

Minimal goodwill on the balance sheet — low impairment risk

sect: Its 32% operating margin is roughly in line with the Financial Services median (29%).
Its share of sector profits slightly exceeds its share of revenue (1.24x).
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+7.9% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.02 across 512 companies in the universe; the top four hold 20% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 43% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 33% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 53% and a beta of 0.93, it moves roughly with the market.
About $15.2M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 40% in the 2020 crash and 45% in the 2022 bear market.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $72.78 (margin of safety -57%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 31%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $54.81 to $99.18 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Financial Services peers: P/E 25.7 vs 12.2, EV/EBITDA 17.0 vs 10.9 and P/FCF 30.6 vs 12.9 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 55% above its 10-year median.
The Street target $160 on average, 40% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
The price implies 20.8% annual cash-flow growth, 9pp more than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 15% earns above the cost of capital of 9.4%, but the 6pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.44).
It converts 34% of revenue into free cash flow.
It earns a 18% return on equity.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 25.2% over 3 years and 18.5% over 5 years, so growth is accelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 25%).
At current returns, reinvesting 60% of profits supports about 9.1% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 7.0% on average.
Analysts expect 4.6% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders own 6.0%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 70%.
Shareholder yield is a modest 1.2% (0.1% in buybacks and 1.8% in dividends).
It has paid a dividend for 12 consecutive years, raising it 7.7% a year over the last five.
people: With about 131 employees, each generates about $2.2M of revenue, 4.3x the Financial Services median, and productivity has risen 18.5% a year.
That works out to $732K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $2.6M (1x revenue per employee).
